tldr: To address the issue where planar AprilTags suffer from severe pose ambiguity in frontal views, the authors developed the "quARtet marker," which tilts four small tags inside a compact footprint. It dramatically reduces near-frontal orientation error from 2.18° to 0.24–0.47° while revealing design trade-offs to keep flat contact surfaces for robot grippers.
hero_caption: Overall workflow of the quARtet marker. A single shared configuration file (setting.json) drives CAD model generation via a Fusion 360 add-in for 3D printing. At detection time, the same parameters reconstruct the 3D corner coordinates to solve a joint 16-point PnP problem, achieving high-accuracy pose estimation without manual calibration.
overview:
In lab automation featuring transparent beakers and reflective tweezers, object recognition and 6-DOF (position and orientation) pose estimation pose major hurdles. Planar AR markers like AprilTags are a practical retrofit because they provide identity and pose simply by being attached. However, they suffer from a fatal geometric weakness: pose estimation accuracy drops significantly when the camera views the marker nearly head-on. In near-frontal views, perspective distortion diminishes, and minor image noise can easily flip the estimated tilt between leaning forward and backward.

While some studies place tags in non-planar configurations to resolve this frontal ambiguity, existing 3D markers have large protrusions that eliminate the flat surfaces required by parallel-jaw grippers. The authors addressed this dilemma with a simple idea: "tilt four small tags in different directions within a single compact footprint." Even when the overall marker faces the camera, each individual tag is observed at an oblique angle, preserving perspective cues.

Embodying this concept as the "quARtet marker," this work proposes three layouts with distinct tilt arrangements. In fixed-camera experiments on a real robot, the proposed marker drastically reduced the mean frontal orientation error from 2.18° for a conventional planar tag down to 0.24–0.47°. Furthermore, swing-down grasping trials on a robot arm demonstrated clear trade-offs: while a centrally peaked layout is most robust across wide viewing angles, it slips easily when grasped; in contrast, stepped pitch layouts retain flat grasping surfaces while preserving high pose accuracy.
contributions: Arranged four tilted AprilTags within the same footprint as a single planar tag (35 mm square) and solved them as a single PnP problem, dramatically improving near-frontal pose estimation accuracy.

Coupled CAD model generation for 3D printing and 3D coordinate reconstruction for the detector through a single shared configuration file, providing an open-source toolchain that works instantly without manual calibration.

Proposed three layouts balancing viewpoint robustness against graspability, and quantitatively evaluated their characteristics through fixed-camera pose estimation and real-robot swing-down grasping experiments.

Conducted closed-loop pose-holding experiments with a hand-eye camera, proving that the proposed marker maintains significantly smaller and more stable errors than conventional tags under visual feedback control.

sections.heading: The pitfall of lab automation: How do we fix markers that wobble when viewed head-on?
sections.summary: Planar AR markers are convenient for lab automation, but pose estimation becomes extremely unstable when viewed head-on because perspective cues vanish. 3D markers solve this, but they create a dilemma by removing flat surfaces needed for robotic grasping.
sections.details:
In automated biological and chemical labs, transparent containers and glossy tools make stable 6-DOF pose estimation with standard RGB-D cameras or depth sensors difficult. Planar fiducial markers like AprilTag or ArUco have long been used as retrofits because they provide both object ID and 6-DOF pose (position and orientation) just by sticking them on, and they can be cheaply replaced when contaminated.

However, there is a well-known geometric trap. Because a square planar tag calculates its tilt from perspective foreshortening of its edges, pose estimation becomes most unstable when the camera is nearly frontal to the tag. A tiny amount of pixel noise can flip the estimated tilt between leaning forward and backward (pose ambiguity). When a robot approaches from above to grasp an object, the camera frequently ends up in this exact frontal view, posing a severe practical problem.

Combining multiple tags into a 3D geometry eliminates this ambiguity, but the resulting protrusions take away the flat contact surfaces parallel-jaw grippers need. Accurate pose estimation and graspability were locked in a trade-off over the same physical surface. To resolve this, the authors designed a novel marker that tilts multiple tags within a compact footprint, retaining oblique perspective cues even in frontal views while preserving graspable surfaces.

captions.F1: Challenges and requirements in robotic lab manipulation. In environments with mixed pipettes and transparent vials (a, b), a marker must simultaneously satisfy four demands: ID recognition, pose accuracy during frontal approach, graspability for grippers, and low-cost 3D printability.

sections.heading: How does it differ from existing 3D markers and detection algorithms?
sections.summary: Efforts to stabilize marker pose estimation fall into two broad categories: 3D geometric shapes and advanced image processing. quARtet stands out by solving the issue purely through geometric design and standard detectors, without requiring specialized optical materials or learned models.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Multi-Tag and 3D Marker Geometry
ChArUco boards and similar planar multi-tag arrangements are widely used for calibration, but as long as the tags remain coplanar, the frontal ambiguity of the overall board persists. The only way to counter this is to enlarge the board, which cannot fit onto small lab tools.

On the other hand, non-planar polyhedral markers and custom markers tailored to object geometries have been explored. However, they often involve complex fabrication or require extra calibration procedures to measure assembly errors between parts, making adoption difficult. quARtet dramatically lowers deployment costs by adopting a compact, plate-like base that can be printed in a single run on standard desktop FDM (Fused Deposition Modeling) 3D printers.

### 2.2 Approaches Extending the Detection Process
Another direction relies on deep-learning-based corner detection or specialized optical markers using lenticular lens arrays or moiré patterns to detect orientation. While highly accurate, these approaches require specialized optical manufacturing or burdensome model retraining for each target.

In contrast, quARtet achieves stability using standard 2D camera images and an off-the-shelf AprilTag detector (pyapriltags), relying entirely on a joint geometric PnP (Perspective-n-Point: solving camera pose from known 3D points and 2D image projections) formulation.

sections.heading: Tilt and solve: The quARtet marker design and its three layouts
sections.summary: quARtet places four small AprilTags tilted at 18 degrees on a 35 mm square base, solving up to 16 detected corners jointly in a single PnP problem. Three layouts—Diagonal, Pitch, and Reversed-Pitch—are provided depending on the use case.
sections.details:
### 3.1 System Overview and Parameter-Coupled Workflow
The overall workflow is shown in Figure F2. A single configuration file, `setting.json`, stores parameters such as the overall marker footprint (35 mm square), individual tag sizes (16 mm square), and the tilt angle (18°). A Fusion 360 add-in reads this file to automatically generate an editable CAD model for 3D printing. At the same time, the detection pipeline reconstructs the 3D corner coordinates from the identical file, eliminating any need to manually measure relative tag positions after printing.

### 3.2 Three Layout Designs
This study implements three layouts differing in how the tags are tilted (Figure F3):
- **quARtet-D (Diagonal)**: Each tag is tilted along its diagonal axis, forming a pyramid-like peak at the center. Because the four tags face outward, they rarely occlude one another and offer uniform visibility from all angles, though virtually no flat grasping surface remains.
- **quARtet-P (Pitch)**: Each tag is tilted about a single bottom axis and arranged in a stepped pattern rotated by 90° successively. This leaves straight, flat contact strips that parallel-jaw gripper fingertips can easily grasp.
- **quARtet-rP (Reversed-Pitch)**: Each block of the Pitch layout is rotated 180° horizontally in place, reversing the tilt direction. This variant offers an alternative balance between graspability and visibility.

Based on simulations, the 18° tilt angle was selected as a sweet spot that resolves frontal ambiguity while keeping overall marker thickness low for ease of fabrication.

### 3.3 Detection and Joint PnP Solving
The corners of each tag (4 tags × 4 corners = up to 16 points) are detected in the image and paired with their known 3D coordinates in the marker frame before making a single call to OpenCV's `solvePnP`. Instead of estimating individual poses and averaging them, solving all corner coordinates jointly in one system of equations strongly suppresses flipped solutions in frontal views. Furthermore, if some tags are occluded by fingers or obstacles, the pose can still be estimated reliably using the remaining tags.

sections.heading: Settling the score: Testing pose accuracy and graspability on real hardware
sections.summary: The authors conducted three evaluations: fixed-camera pose estimation, closed-loop pose-holding with an arm-mounted camera, and grasping stability tests under vigorous arm swing-downs. The proposed method reduced frontal angular error by about 9x, while grasping slip varied by a factor of 100 depending on the layout.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Common Hardware Setup
A conventional single planar tag (Single) with the same 35 mm square footprint served as the baseline. The three quARtet layouts (D, P, rP) used four 16 mm tag36h11 markers with an 18° base tilt. Experiments utilized a UR5e robot arm and an industrial Keyence IV4 camera.

### 4.2 Pose Estimation and Closed-Loop Evaluation (RQ1)
Markers were attached to the robot tool flange and positioned about 220 mm from a fixed camera while varying their pose (Figure F4).
- **Orientation Error**: As shown in Figure F6, the conventional Single tag exhibited a large mean angular error of 2.18° (standard deviation 0.80°) in the frontal view (center cell). In contrast, quARtet-D reduced this to 0.24°, P to 0.27°, and rP to 0.47°—suppressing error by roughly 5x to 9x. In oblique views (±30°), P and rP experienced minor accuracy drops due to self-occlusion, whereas quARtet-D remained the most stable overall, keeping error under 0.8° across all tested angles.
- **Position Error**: In translation tests (Figure F7), the root-mean-square error (RMSE) was 1.50 mm for the Single tag, whereas all three quARtet layouts significantly improved to 0.17–0.20 mm.
- **Closed-Loop Pose Holding**: With the camera mounted on the robot arm looking down at the marker, visual feedback control was run for 120 seconds (Figure F5). As shown in Figure F8, the Single tag oscillated with a mean error of 0.68° (step-to-step fluctuation 0.31°), while all quARtet layouts maintained the target pose extremely smoothly with mean errors of 0.08–0.11° (fluctuations 0.05–0.10°, adjusted $p < 10^{-4}$ via Welch's t-test).

### 4.3 Graspability Evaluation (RQ2)
Markers were attached to both ends of a cuboid block and gripped directly over the marker faces using a Robotiq 2F-140 parallel-jaw gripper. The arm was swung down abruptly over a 50° amplitude at an angular velocity of roughly 180 deg/s, and in-grasp slip was measured using an OptiTrack motion capture system.
- **Results**: Lacking flat contact surfaces, quARtet-D could not withstand the dynamic forces, slipping by an average of 103.53 mm and rotating 24.85° (an effective grasp failure). In contrast, quARtet-P and quARtet-rP, which preserve flat contact strips, slipped by only 1.02 mm and 2.02 mm respectively. Compared to the completely flat Single tag (0.33 mm slip), they securely held the object with only about 1 mm of additional slip.

sections.heading: Which one should you pick? Decision rules for layout selection
sections.summary: Experimental findings yield a clear operational rule: choose quARtet-D when viewpoint-consistent pose estimation dominates, and choose a pitch-based layout (P or rP) when the marker face itself must remain graspable by a robot hand.
sections.details:
The key achievement of this work is not just creating a high-accuracy marker, but quantitatively highlighting the trade-off between geometric pose-estimation consistency and mechanical graspability.

quARtet-D features four tags flared outward symmetrically, minimizing mutual shadowing and providing rich perspective cues from almost any viewing angle. Therefore, when there is no need to grasp the marked face itself—such as fixed reference markers on a workbench or the top surface of tools that have separate grasp handles—quARtet-D is without question the best choice.

Conversely, when manipulating pipettes or small vials where the gripper must squeeze the exact face where the marker is placed, quARtet-P and quARtet-rP shine. Although they suffer slight blind spots at oblique angles where adjacent tags cast shadows, their frontal pose accuracy remains vastly superior to a single planar tag, and their flat strips provide a graspable surface capable of enduring aggressive arm motions with only around 1 mm of slip.

There are limitations. The current evaluation is restricted to a specific marker footprint (35 mm square) and a specific gripper, without evaluating full task-level success rates such as complete pick-and-place routines. Additionally, fixed-camera experiments used the robot's commanded poses as the reference baseline, meaning the results demonstrate relative consistency under identical conditions rather than certified absolute ground truth.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook
sections.summary: The quARtet marker resolves frontal pose estimation ambiguity by solving four tilted tags jointly, while allowing users to balance graspability through layout selection. With an open-source toolchain linking CAD to detection, it is a practical technology ready for immediate lab automation deployment.
sections.details:
This paper presented quARtet, a 3D-printable fiducial marker that combines four tilted AprilTags within a compact footprint and solves their pose as a single PnP problem. It dramatically reduces near-frontal angular and position errors, proving its superiority even under closed-loop control.

Furthermore, by clarifying the trade-offs between pitch layouts that preserve flat grasping surfaces and the diagonal layout tailored for viewpoint robustness, the authors established clear design guidelines for practical applications. All code, CAD add-ins, and experimental datasets are available on GitHub.

Future work includes evaluating the marker in end-to-end manipulation tasks like reagent pipetting and labware transport, testing simultaneous multi-marker detection within a shared field of view, and verifying robustness under severe occlusion scenarios.

takeaways: Planar AR markers are most vulnerable to pose flipping when viewed near-frontally, making even slight tag tilt exceptionally effective.
Arranging multiple tilted tags within a compact footprint and solving all corner coordinates in a single joint PnP problem improves orientation accuracy roughly ninefold without additional hardware.

Making markers three-dimensional removes flat contact surfaces for robot grippers, making it crucial to choose pitch-based layouts with flat strips when grasping is required, and symmetric diagonal layouts when it is not.
limitations: Because robot commanded poses (repeatability ±0.03 mm) served as the reference in fixed-camera experiments, pose accuracy was evaluated relatively rather than against certified absolute ground truth.
Fitting four smaller 16 mm tags into a 35 mm footprint reduces the maximum detection range compared to a single full-sized 35 mm planar tag.
In pitch-based layouts, raised surfaces can partially occlude tags behind them when viewed obliquely, leading to a slight drop in accuracy at specific tilt angles.
